explain.say: Paper is a mat of tiny plant fibres, mostly from wood, tangled and bonded together. First logs are chipped, then cooked with chemicals or ground up to free the fibres into a soggy porridge called pulp.

explain.say: Rollers press out more water, then the sheet snakes around dozens of steam-heated drums until it is dry. As it dries, the fibres bond together, and that is what holds paper together.

faq.a: Wood pulp is wood broken down into its separate cellulose fibres, mixed with water. Chemical pulping cooks wood chips to dissolve the lignin glue between fibres; mechanical pulping grinds them apart.
asks: How is wood turned into paper?

faq.q: How does pulp become a sheet of paper?
faq.a: Very watery pulp is spread onto a moving mesh. As the water drains, the fibres settle and tangle into a sheet, which is then pressed and dried on heated rollers. Modern machines run at over 100 kilometres an hour.
asks: How does a paper machine work?

faq.a: Cellulose fibres are covered in tiny chemical groups that form hydrogen bonds with each other as the water dries out. Millions of these bonds where fibres touch hold the sheet together. Add water and they let go, which is why wet paper tears easily.
asks: Why does wet paper fall apart?

faq.q: How many times can paper be recycled?
faq.a: Usually about five to seven times. Each time it is pulped, the fibres get shorter and weaker, until they are too short to bond into a sheet, so some new fibre is always mixed in.
Paper was invented in China; an official named Cai Lun is credited with improving papermaking around 105 CE using bark, hemp and rags. The skill later spread through the Islamic world to Europe.

facts: Cai Lun is credited with improving papermaking in China around 105 CE.
Paper fibres can typically be recycled about five to seven times.

options.show: The fibres get shorter each time

quiz.why: Each pulping shortens the fibres until they are too short to bond into a sheet.
